title: Fellow hobbyist solo devs, how do you handle your game's art without spending a fortune?
author: championgame42
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I have a question for fellow solo developers who, like me, make games mainly out of passion, just for the fun of bringing their ideas to life and sharing them with the world.

**How do you handle the visual side of your games?**

I've realized that even when a game has interesting gameplay, a lot of players will judge it based on its visuals before giving it a chance. This seems especially true when the art has that easily recognizable AI-generated look.

The problem is, I'm neither an artist nor an illustrator. I can spend hundreds of hours developing a game, but I honestly can't justify spending thousands of euros on artwork for a hobby project that will probably never make any money.

And I completely understand the criticism of AI-generated art, especially when it comes to consistency and the lack of a unique visual identity.

But for a solo developer with no drawing skills and a limited budget, **what are the realistic alternatives?**

I'm curious about your approaches:

* Do you learn to draw and create everything yourself?
* Do you use asset packs and customize them?
* Do you hire artists despite having a small budget?
* Have you found any other tricks to create a consistent and recognizable art style without spending a fortune?

My goal isn't necessarily to make a commercially successful game. I just want to create something fun, give it its own identity, and hopefully get people interested enough to try out my ideas.

**So, how do you guys approach this? I'd genuinely love to hear about your experiences, methods, and tips!**

replies.author: ThePhallusofGod
replies.body:
Make a tool for it.
I used chatgpt astra to make a seamless texture generator that works at any resolution. I gave it examples of what i want and kept telling it to keep working until it looked as good as I want. I'd point things out like... Your image is lacking the contrast of this image, the colour vibrancy etc.
I got some pretty cool results, and if you're clever about it you can hop on and edit the generated textures.
It's more fun and the results are better than image gen.

replies.author: loopywolf
replies.body: It sounds like that's a tool for a background texture generator.  Does it work when you want to make tiles for a mountain? or a base?

replies.author: ThePhallusofGod
replies.body:
I can make base textures yes, bricks, tiles, concrete, piping. I used doom textures as a reference to see how close i could get. It loops them seamlessly from the start. I focused mostly on low res stuff because it's what I like, and with that purpose in mind it's great - you can download it and tweak it yourself.
I don't have mountain rocks specifically but there's plenty of rocky stuff it can do.

Ask you agent and they'll make it! I keep forgetting with llms... If you can imagine it, it can more or less build it

I'd tell astra or opus 5.5 to "make me a seamlessly looping texture generator application that runs in the browser. It creates images at custom resolutions based on reference images I send you. I would like several presets - mountain tiles (side on, top down?), mountains with bases, etc etc. Allow the images to be resized dynamically and not generated at one set resolution, allow them to be edited layer by layer with all the controls you used to create them... Brightness, contrast, warping, texture generating, noise patterns etc."
I got lazy writing that prompt but it's more or less it. Give it some references in the code session/chat and you'll be good to begin after some back and forth.

comments.author: ThePhallusofGod
comments.body:
I don't particularly like AI art, and I like to have more control over the audiovisual identity of my game.
I've been focusing on only creating withing my means - but obviously with AI tools assisting.
My game has pixel art - 32x32 sprites and textures, and sdf/vector assets (all with the same pixel resolution for consistency).
It's been gratifying drawing my sprites the best I can - and I think you could find with some tools like auto shading, and assistance with drawing you could make yourself a tool to teach you how to make the art you want.
Easy for me to say because my vision is pixelly assets, if you're dreaming bigger and better that's tougher.

If it were me drawing detailed 2d assets I would make a tool to draw that helps my shortcomings.
Perspective, proportions... I'd use AI to put overlays on the canvas that help me, use processes like normal mapping for shading, use best practices for colour selection, and defining colour elements across the game so things pop when you want them to.

You can make a tool that helps all the gaps in your knowledge, instead of battling with image gen that never quite gets it.

You could use a hybrid approach too, generate rough art - drop it in your editor and edit by hand. Use the tools to help along the way.

Good luck

replies.author: championgame42

replies.author: ZymzAlchemy
replies.body:
I try to craft as much of it on my own as I can, less concerned about AI and more about adhering to my desired aesthetic. 

But even as a beginning you can make rudimentary sketches and feed them to your agent as references for layouts or sprite design to guide it in the right direction. This is especially useful with SOL (Codex). I feed it a single reference sketch and then a sheet of stick figures for animations and it maps my reference art over the stick figures to get the animation sheets I need. 

So my best advice is do as much as you can, and always strive to learn more. Even after more than 40 years in tech, I learn something new every day. 

Be well and keep creating.

comments.author: Felmeric
comments.body:
For 2d art I use game labs studio. I find it's quite cheap and produces good art that can easily be used in games. I get claude to manage it using an mcp connection so if I need to change anything the prompt it sends stays consistent. 

If I need 3d models, I run a local llm set up that takes 2d images and builds them into 3d models using Hunyuan3D-2. It takes in a reference image and the makes a textured model from that. You can even give it multimedia reference images but it will only use the textured data from one. 
It normally does a very good job even on my low end machine. I just asked claude to set it up and it took care of the rest. 

Setting up blender mcp also let's claude code do a lot of work on simple models. It works best when it has actual dimensions to deal with. At first it didn't want to texture the models but there is no reason it can't, I just had to ask and it started doing it.

comments.author: Ill-Ant-9489
comments.body: A thing I built might fit here, so heads up that it is mine: LoRA Dataset Studio, free and local, https://github.com/perfectgf/lora-dataset-studio. The obvious AI look is mostly the base model's averaged style bleeding through, and the fix is the route you already settled on, lock one look and make everything bend to it. That is what a style LoRA does. You train it once on 15 to 25 images in your chosen style, pulled from your best outputs or one cheap asset pack, and then every sprite and background lands in that style instead of generic gen. LDS preps the set and writes the ai-toolkit recipe, and there is a rent-a-GPU step if your card cannot train locally. What engine are you building in, pixel art or something more painterly?

replies.author: championgame42
replies.body: Thanks for sharing! I'll definitely check it out. i am working in a card game built entirely in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, without a game engine. Since it's a card game, illustrations are a huge part of the visual experience. I'm aiming for a hand-drawn comic-book style, and my biggest challenge is keeping the artwork consistent without that obvious AI look.

replies.author: Ill-Ant-9489
replies.body:
One hand-drawn look across all the cards is really a style LoRA job, not per card prompting, which is the whole point of my project, https://github.com/perfectgf/lora-dataset-studio.

Train it on a tight set of the comic style you want, consistent linework and shading, and every card inherits it. The plastic AI look usually comes from the base, so keep strength moderate and it stays drawn. How many style refs do you have to work from?

comments.author: Dismal-Confidence858
comments.body:
I used to create 2d rigs from concept art, that I would render at low resolution with a limited color palette. I used the tool pixelover for this, which is pretty good for this workflow.

Now I am moving to low poly models in blender, that I animate there. What allowed me to make this move was a subscription to Claude, which can build decent models using blender.

If you want to see what it looks like, my game is here : https://mofleury.itch.io/fairies-will . The screenshots are still the pixelover version, the game is using the 3d models for most of the art, I still have a few sprites that I have not ported yet.

Note that I tried to find ways to get ai to create animations by creating sprite sheets directly, and I am pretty sure that it is not the way, because good animations require precise timing, and you need to have full control over it. Maybe products like pixel lab can help on this front, I have not tried, I prefer to avoid paying too many subscriptions...

I hope this helps!

comments.author: Prof_Utoniu
comments.body:
Hi, here's some stuff I use for my 3D project:

	•	Comfy + MCP Blender for generating/polishing assets. For complex assets I had Claude break the asset into components and make reference sheets for each one, then render and put them together in Blender. I've also got a pipeline built around what I've made so far, the art style I'm going for and textures from my library. Even with a good pipeline you'll still have to iterate a few times.  
	•	Found a lot of free assets but recently I bought like 3 mega bundle packs with lots of studio quality levels, textures, tools and a few premium subs ($70 total and I'm stopping there since it's just a hobby, not trying to sell anything). I customise some of the levels for my project and pull a bunch of elements from them into my library and pipelines.  
	•	Built an in-game tool for placing assets since Claude isn't great at "place a settlement/village/city", then he can anchor and polish them.  
  
I think for a long-term hobby or commercial purpose it really helps to actually have some skills so you can make/polish assets, create scenes and a credible environment overall.
